headings.title: Definition and Diagnostic Criteria of Preterm Labour
headings.content: Preterm labour is officially defined by the World Health Organization (WHO) and professional bodies in Nigeria as the onset of regular uterine contractions resulting in progressive cervical change occurring between 22 completed weeks and 36 completed weeks plus 6 days of gestation. This distinction is vital in nursing practice because neonates born before 37 weeks face significantly higher risks of prematurity-related complications compared to term infants. To establish a definitive diagnosis of preterm labour, specific clinical criteria must be met. These criteria include documented persistent uterine contractions occurring at a frequency of at least four contractions every 20 minutes, or eight contractions in 60 minutes, accompanied by progressive cervical effacement of 80% or greater, and cervical dilation of 2 cm or more. In clinical settings across Nigeria, accurate gestational age dating—determined via early ultrasound or a reliable last menstrual period—is foundational for diagnosis. If contractions are present but cervical changes are absent, the condition is often classified as threatened preterm labour, requiring close observation rather than immediate aggressive intervention. Nursing students must remember that differentiating true preterm labour from false labour or braxton hicks contractions prevents unnecessary hospital admissions and inappropriate medical treatments while ensuring timely intervention when genuine preterm labour occurs.

headings.title: Etiology and Risk Factors for Preterm Birth
headings.content: Understanding the etiology and risk factors associated with preterm birth is essential for early identification and preventive care in obstetric nursing. Preterm births can be categorized into spontaneous preterm labour, preterm premature rupture of membranes (PPROM), and provider-initiated (indicated) preterm delivery due to maternal or fetal complications. Multiple risk factors contribute to these classifications and are frequently encountered in Nigerian healthcare facilities. A primary risk factor is a history of a previous preterm delivery, which significantly increases the likelihood of recurrence in subsequent pregnancies. Other maternal risk factors include multiple gestations (such as twins or triplets), uterine anomalies, cervical incompetence, low pre-pregnancy body mass index, short interpregnancy intervals, and extremes of maternal age. Infections are also a major precipitating factor, particularly urinary tract infections, bacterial vaginosis, and sexually transmitted infections, which trigger inflammatory cascades leading to uterine contractions. Socioeconomic factors, poor antenatal attendance, high physical stress, and maternal chronic medical conditions like hypertension and diabetes further elevate risk. Student nurses must perform thorough risk assessments during antenatal care visits to identify vulnerable women early and implement preventive strategies such as progesterone supplementation or lifestyle counseling.

headings.title: Pathophysiology and Mechanisms of Preterm Initiation
headings.content: The pathophysiology underlying the initiation of preterm labour shares many common pathways with term labour, albeit activated prematurely. These pathways involve a complex network of endocrine, inflammatory, and mechanical signals that lead to activation of the myometrium, cervical ripening, and rupture of fetal membranes. A central mechanism is the functional withdrawal of progesterone, which normally maintains uterine quiescence by suppressing contraction-associated proteins. When progesterone levels drop or its receptor sensitivity decreases, estrogen dominance takes over, upregulating myometrial oxytocin receptors and gap junctions. Additionally, intrauterine infection and inflammation play a critical role; pro-inflammatory cytokines such as interleukin-1 beta, interleukin-6, and tumor necrosis factor-alpha stimulate the production of prostaglandins. These prostaglandins act locally to promote cervical softening and stimulate myometrial contractions. Mechanical stretching of the uterus, commonly seen in polyhydramnios or multiple gestations, also triggers local upregulation of contraction pathways. Furthermore, decidual hemorrhage and activation of the coagulation cascade can initiate early membrane rupture and labour. For nursing students, grasping these biochemical and physiological processes helps clarify why specific interventions—like tocolytics or antibiotics—are chosen to counteract these exact mechanisms during clinical management.

headings.title: Clinical Assessment and Diagnostic Evaluation
headings.content: Clinical assessment and diagnostic evaluation of a pregnant woman presenting with suspected preterm labour require a systematic, calm, and thorough approach by the nursing and medical team. The initial nursing assessment involves gathering a detailed obstetric history, noting the exact gestational age, characteristics of contractions, presence of vaginal bleeding, fluid leakage, or symptoms of urinary tract infections. Vital signs must be monitored promptly to rule out maternal systemic infection or distress. Physical examination includes abdominal palpation to assess fetal lie, presentation, and uterine tenderness, followed by a sterile speculum examination to inspect the cervix, visualize fluid pooling, and obtain samples for diagnostic tests. Digital vaginal examinations should be minimized or avoided if placenta previa or preterm premature rupture of membranes is suspected, to prevent introducing infection or triggering hemorrhage. Diagnostic evaluations commonly utilized include cervical length measurement via transvaginal ultrasound, where a shortened cervix (typically less than 25 mm) strongly predicts preterm birth. Additionally, fetal fibronectin (fFN) tests can be performed; a negative fFN result has a high negative predictive value, indicating that delivery within the next two weeks is unlikely. Laboratory investigations such as complete blood count, urinalysis, and high vaginal swabs help identify underlying infectious etiologies that require targeted antibiotic therapy.

headings.title: Pharmacological Management and Tocolytic Therapy
headings.content: Pharmacological management of preterm labour primarily focuses on the use of tocolytic therapy. Tocolytics are medications administered to suppress uterine contractions, temporarily halting labour. The primary goal of tocolysis is not to stop labour permanently, but rather to buy crucial time—typically 48 hours—allowing for the administration of maternal corticosteroids to accelerate fetal lung maturation and to facilitate safe transfer of the mother to a tertiary health facility with neonatal intensive care capabilities, a common scenario in Nigerian obstetric care. Commonly used tocolytics include calcium channel blockers (such as nifedipine), oxytocin receptor antagonists (such as atosiban), beta-adrenergic agonists (such as ritodrine or terbutaline), and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (such as indomethacin). Nifedipine is frequently preferred due to its favorable maternal side effect profile and ease of administration. Contraindications to tocolytic therapy must be strictly observed by nurses; they include intrauterine fetal demise, lethal fetal anomalies, severe chorioamnionitis, maternal hemodynamic instability, severe preeclampsia, or advanced cervical dilation (usually greater than 4 cm), where tocolysis would be ineffective or hazardous. Nurses play a crucial role in monitoring maternal vital signs, tracking intake and output, assessing for adverse drug reactions (such as hypotension with nifedipine or pulmonary edema with beta-agonists), and continuously monitoring fetal heart rate patterns during therapy.

headings.title: Fetal Lung Maturation and Corticosteroid Administration
headings.content: Fetal lung immaturity is the leading cause of morbidity and mortality in preterm neonates, manifesting clinically as respiratory distress syndrome (RDS). To mitigate this, antenatal corticosteroid administration is one of the most effective interventions in modern obstetrics. Corticosteroids—specifically dexamethasone or betamethasone—accelerate the structural and functional maturation of the fetal lungs by stimulating the synthesis and release of pulmonary surfactant, reducing alveolar surface tension, and improving lung compliance. According to international and Nigerian obstetric guidelines, a course of antenatal corticosteroids is indicated for pregnant women between 24 and 34 weeks of gestation who are at risk of preterm delivery within the next seven days. The standard regimen for betamethasone is two doses of 12 mg administered intramuscularly 24 hours apart, while dexamethasone is given as four doses of 6 mg intramuscularly every 12 hours. Nurses must administer these injections precisely on schedule and educate mothers on their purpose. In addition to reducing RDS, corticosteroids significantly lower the incidence of intraventricular hemorrhage and necrotizing enterocolitis in the newborn. Nurses must also monitor diabetic mothers closely during corticosteroid therapy, as these medications can transiently elevate maternal blood glucose levels, requiring adjustments in insulin or glycemic management.

headings.title: Intrapartum Care and Delivery Management
headings.content: Intrapartum care and delivery management for a preterm fetus demand specialized skills and interprofessional collaboration between midwives, obstetricians, and pediatric/neonatal teams. When delivery becomes inevitable, the mode of delivery—vaginal versus Cesarean section—must be individualized based on gestational age, fetal presentation, and maternal indications. While vertex presentations at very early gestational ages may be delivered vaginally with careful monitoring, breech presentations or extreme prematurity often warrant a Cesarean section to minimize mechanical trauma to the fragile fetal head. Throughout the first and second stages of labour, continuous electronic fetal monitoring (EFM) is vital because preterm infants tolerate hypoxia and uterine contractions poorly. The nurse must watch closely for signs of fetal distress, such as late or severe variable decelerations. During the second stage, controlled delivery of the head may be performed, and routine prophylactic episiotomy may be considered to reduce intracranial pressure in extremely preterm infants, though current practices favor individualized decisions. Crucially, a qualified neonatal resuscitation team must be present at every preterm birth, equipped with appropriate-sized masks, endotracheal tubes, and radiant warmers to provide immediate thermal regulation and respiratory support as soon as the baby is born.

headings.title: Complications and Neonatal Prognosis
headings.content: Complications associated with preterm birth significantly impact neonatal morbidity and long-term prognosis, presenting major challenges in pediatric and nursing practice. The severity of these complications is inversely proportional to gestational age and birth weight. Immediate neonatal complications include respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) due to surfactant deficiency, transient tachypnea, and bronchopulmonary dysplasia. Neurological complications are frequent, notably intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH) and periventricular leukomalacia, which can result from fluctuations in cerebral blood flow and fragile germinal matrix vessels. Gastrointestinal systems are similarly immature, placing the preterm neonate at high risk for necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC), a devastating ischemic and inflammatory bowel necrosis often linked to early enteral feeding. Other acute issues include hyperbilirubinemia, hypothermia, hypoglycemia, and sepsis due to immature immune function. Long-term prognoses may involve chronic respiratory conditions, neurodevelopmental delays, cerebral palsy, visual impairments like retinopathy of prematurity (ROP), and hearing loss. For nursing students, understanding these complications highlights the importance of meticulous neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) nursing, developmental positioning, infection control, and supportive family-centered care to improve survival and quality of life outcomes for preterm infants.

headings.title: Nursing Interventions and Maternal Support
headings.content: Nursing interventions and maternal support form the backbone of holistic care for women experiencing preterm labour and their families. Because preterm labour is often sudden and unexpected, mothers and families experience intense anxiety, fear, guilt, and emotional trauma regarding the health and survival of their unborn child. Nurses must provide empathetic psychological support, clear communication, and continuous reassurance, explaining every procedure and care plan step-by-step. Physical nursing interventions include maintaining strict bed rest in a lateral recumbent position to enhance uteroplacental perfusion, administering prescribed tocolytics and corticosteroids while monitoring for adverse effects, and keeping accurate fluid balance charts. Pain management techniques, emotional presence, and relaxation encouragement help reduce stress hormones that can further stimulate uterine activity. In cases where delivery occurs, nurses facilitate early maternal-infant bonding, kangaroo mother care (KMC) when the infant is stable, and lactation support for expressing breast milk, which is crucial for preventing NEC and boosting infant immunity. Furthermore, culturally sensitive counseling and discharge education prepare parents for the realities of NICU care and follow-up appointments, empowering them to actively participate in their newborn's recovery journey in Nigerian healthcare settings.
